Chapter 1 · pages 23–36

Retrieving Records

The retrieval foundation: selecting rows and columns, naming results, concatenating values, applying conditional logic, limiting output, and handling NULLs and patterns.

What this chapter solves

Chapter 1 establishes the vocabulary of retrieval: choose rows, choose columns, name the result, and handle the awkward cases (NULLs, patterns, limits, and randomness).

  • Read every row or apply a predicate with WHERE.
  • Project only the columns the caller needs.
  • Turn raw column names into readable labels.
  • Shape values with concatenation and conditional logic.

Core techniques

  • Filter early: put row criteria in WHERE before sorting or aggregating.
  • Alias carefully: an alias is for the result set; databases generally will not accept it in the same query’s WHERE clause.
  • Limit explicitly: use the dialect’s row-limit syntax when any n rows are acceptable.
  • Make NULL visible: test with IS NULL and replace with COALESCE/ISNULL/NVL.

Dialect differences to expect

  • Concatenation: || (Oracle, PostgreSQL, DB2), + (SQL Server), CONCAT() (MySQL).
  • Row limits: FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY, LIMIT n, or TOP n.
  • Random ordering: RAND(), RANDOM(), NEWID(), or DBMS_RANDOM.VALUE.
  • Pattern matching: LIKE is portable, but case sensitivity and escape characters vary.

Common traps

  • Using an alias in WHERE and being surprised by a syntax error.
  • Assuming NULL = NULL; use IS NULL instead.
  • Using TOP/LIMIT without ORDER BY when the result must be repeatable.
  • Matching patterns accidentally: % and _ are wildcards, not literals.

Representative pattern

Filter first, then shape the projection. When a derived name must be filtered, wrap the query in an inline view (or repeat the expression) so the outer WHERE sees a real column.

select deptno,
       count(*) as headcount
  from (select deptno, sal
          from emp
         where sal > 1000) as x
 group by deptno
having count(*) > 1;

Book insight: the authors treat these “simple” recipes as the foundation of everything else in the book. A retrieval mistake is amplified later by joins, grouping, and reporting.

Takeaway: think in three passes—filter rows, shape columns, then order/limit. Keep expressions portable by isolating dialect-specific functions in small, replaceable pieces.

Chapter 2 · pages 37–50

Sorting Query Results

ORDER BY basics and the details that make ordering reliable: multiple keys, substrings, mixed alphanumeric values, NULLs, and data-dependent sort orders.

What this chapter solves

Sorting is where a query stops being a bag of rows and becomes a report. Chapter 2 covers deterministic ordering, multi-key sorts, ordering parts of a value, and the awkward behavior of NULLs.

  • Sort by one key or a chain of keys.
  • Order by a substring or a numeric portion hidden inside text.
  • Decide where NULLs belong in the output.
  • Build keys whose order depends on the data itself.

Core techniques

  • ORDER BY accepts expressions, aliases (in most dialects), and ordinal positions.
  • Add a unique trailing key so equal primary keys never reorder unpredictably.
  • Use SUBSTRING/INSTR to expose a sortable component.
  • Use a CASE expression to turn a business rule into a sort key.

Dialect differences to expect

  • NULL placement: NULLS FIRST/NULLS LAST where supported; otherwise emulate with CASE.
  • Case/accent collations can change the perceived order of strings.
  • Some engines reject ordinal ORDER BY positions in views or DISTINCT queries.
  • Random sort is deliberately non-deterministic; see Chapter 1 for random row selection.

Common traps

  • Sorting only by a non-unique key and seeing rows “shuffle” between runs.
  • Sorting mixed alphanumeric data as text, so “100” lands before “20”.
  • Assuming every database puts NULLs in the same place.
  • Sorting an alias in a context where the dialect requires the underlying expression.

Representative pattern

When a visible value is not sortable, derive a key, sort by the key, and return the readable value. A data-dependent key can also encode a priority such as “active first, then alphabetical.”

select ename, sal, comm
  from emp
 order by case when comm is null then 1 else 0 end,
          comm desc,
          ename;

Book insight: the chapter’s closing note emphasizes that ORDER BY is powerful but nuanced. Later recipes repeatedly rely on a stable, intentional sort order.

Takeaway: never let the database invent an order. Make every sort explicit, put a unique tie-breaker last, and treat NULL placement as a design decision rather than an accident.

Chapter 3 · pages 51–88

Working with Multiple Tables

Joins, set operations, anti-joins, table comparisons, Cartesian-product detection, and the interaction between joins and aggregation.

What this chapter solves

Chapter 3 moves from single-table queries to relationships: stack compatible result sets, join related rows, find matches and non-matches, and keep aggregates correct when several tables are involved.

  • Combine rows with UNION/UNION ALL.
  • Join on shared keys without creating accidental Cartesian products.
  • Find rows present in one table but missing from another.
  • Compare tables, including their cardinality and values.

Core techniques

  • Inner join: keep only matching pairs.
  • Outer join: preserve one side, then filter it with IS NULL for anti-joins.
  • Set comparison: use INTERSECT/EXCEPT where available, or two-sided joins.
  • Aggregate after shaping: pre-aggregate or use DISTINCT when a join multiplies rows.

Dialect differences to expect

  • FULL OUTER JOIN support and syntax differ across older engines.
  • NOT IN changes behavior when the subquery can return NULL; NOT EXISTS is often safer.
  • UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL preserves them and is usually cheaper.
  • Some databases require derived tables/views to be aliased for joins.

Common traps

  • Joining two unrelated columns and producing a many-to-many explosion.
  • Joining before aggregation and silently multiplying totals.
  • Using NOT IN with a nullable list and getting an empty result.
  • Forgetting that NULL never equals another value, including itself.

Representative pattern

An outer join plus a NULL test is the portable anti-join. It answers “which departments have no employees?” without relying on dialect-specific set operators.

select d.deptno, d.dname
  from dept d
  left join emp e
    on e.deptno = d.deptno
 where e.empno is null;

Book insight: the recipes repeatedly separate “find the rows” from “format the rows.” Keeping those stages distinct makes joins, outer joins, and aggregates much easier to debug.

Takeaway: decide the row relationship first (one-to-one, one-to-many, or “missing from”), then choose the join. Check row counts after every join before you trust an aggregate.

Chapter 4 · pages 89–112

Inserting, Updating, and Deleting

Practical DML: inserts with defaults and copied rows, safe updates, merge-style changes, and deletes scoped by keys, predicates, or integrity rules.

What this chapter solves

Chapter 4 covers the write side of SQL: insert new rows, copy data, apply defaults and constraints, update matched sets, merge changes, and delete safely.

  • Insert literals, defaults, NULL overrides, and query results.
  • Copy a table’s definition or its rows.
  • Update with predicates, joins, or a merge operation.
  • Delete everything, selected rows, duplicates, or integrity violations.

Core techniques

  • Make the WHERE clause of every UPDATE/DELETE reviewable with a SELECT first.
  • Use defaults intentionally; an omitted column is not the same as an explicit NULL in every schema.
  • Use INSERT ... SELECT for set-based copying.
  • Use MERGE (or equivalent insert/update logic) when a row may or may not exist.

Dialect differences to expect

  • Multi-table insert syntax is vendor-specific.
  • MERGE semantics and concurrency guarantees differ by engine.
  • Deleting duplicates may require a temporary key or window function.
  • Triggers, identity columns, and generated columns can change what a “simple” insert does.

Common traps

  • Omitting WHERE and changing or deleting the whole table.
  • Copying rows without matching column order or default rules.
  • Updating through a join that produces duplicate matches.
  • Deleting child rows before their parent, violating referential integrity.

Representative pattern

Preview the target set, then run the same predicate in the modification statement. This is the book’s safety habit for every destructive operation.

-- preview
select empno, ename, deptno
  from emp
 where deptno = 10;

-- apply only after the preview looks right
delete from emp
 where deptno = 10;

Book insight: the chapter treats deletion as a question of scope. Primary and unique keys are the safest way to narrow that scope to exactly one row.

Takeaway: data changes are set operations. Define the set with a read-only query, verify it, then apply the write inside a transaction whenever the database supports one.

Chapter 5 · pages 113–126

Metadata Queries

Schema introspection with SQL: tables, columns, indexes, constraints, missing foreign-key indexes, and dynamically generated maintenance statements.

What this chapter solves

Chapter 5 uses SQL to inspect SQL: list tables, columns, indexes, constraints, and foreign keys, then generate maintenance SQL from the metadata itself.

  • Find the tables in a schema.
  • Describe a table’s columns and data types.
  • Locate indexes and constraints, including missing foreign-key indexes.
  • Generate statements from catalog/data-dictionary views.

Core techniques

  • INFORMATION_SCHEMA is the portable starting point where supported.
  • System catalogs (Oracle data dictionary, PostgreSQL catalogs, SQL Server system views) expose deeper details.
  • Concatenate catalog rows to build CREATE/ALTER scripts.
  • Join metadata views to compare declared constraints with actual indexes.

Dialect differences to expect

  • Oracle’s dictionary views (USER_TABLES, USER_TAB_COLUMNS, etc.) differ from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.
  • Index and constraint names are not standardized across engines.
  • Some metadata is available only through vendor-specific procedures.
  • Permissions may hide tables or columns from the current user.

Common traps

  • Assuming a foreign key always has a supporting index.
  • Confusing a unique constraint with a primary key.
  • Hard-coding catalog names that only work in one database.
  • Generating SQL without checking the current schema/search path.

Representative pattern

A portable column inventory is often as simple as filtering INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS by table name and sorting by ordinal position.

select column_name, data_type, is_nullable, ordinal_position
  from information_schema.columns
 where table_schema = 'public'
   and table_name   = 'emp'
 order by ordinal_position;

Book insight: metadata queries are especially useful when you inherit an unfamiliar database. The same techniques support audits, documentation, and automated schema reviews.

Takeaway: learn one portable metadata interface and one vendor catalog. With both, you can answer “what is this table?” without leaving SQL.

Chapter 6 · pages 127–190

Working with Strings

A broad string toolbox: character walking, quote handling, cleaning, separation, delimited lists, initials, ordering, IP parsing, soundex matching, and negative patterns.

What this chapter solves

Chapter 6 treats text as data: walk through a string, clean it, separate numeric and alphabetic pieces, build and parse delimited lists, and search by pattern or sound.

  • Count, remove, and replace characters.
  • Extract initials, substrings, and the nth delimited field.
  • Convert a delimited list to an IN-list and back again.
  • Handle alphanumeric mixtures, IP addresses, and phonetic matches.

Core techniques

  • Recursive CTEs can consume a string one character or one delimiter at a time.
  • SUBSTRING/SUBSTR, INSTR/POSITION, and REPLACE form the portable toolkit.
  • LIKE and regular expressions handle pattern questions; use NOT LIKE for exclusions.
  • SOUNDEX or vendor equivalents support approximate name matching.

Dialect differences to expect

  • String indexes are 1-based in some engines and 0-based in others.
  • Concatenation and quote-escaping rules differ (single quotes doubled vs. backslash escapes).
  • Regular-expression functions are not universally available.
  • TRIM, REPLACE, and case-folding behavior vary by collation.

Common traps

  • Forgetting the empty trailing field when a delimiter ends the string.
  • Removing “non-numeric” characters with a character set that also removes signs or decimal points unintentionally.
  • Assuming a pattern is case-sensitive in every database.
  • Splitting text with SUBSTRING alone when delimiters can repeat.

Representative pattern

For a simple comma-separated list, a recursive CTE can produce one row per element. The same skeleton scales to log lines, serialized records, or any repeated delimiter.

with parts (value, rest) as (
  select '', 'a,b,c'
  union all
  select left(rest, case when position(',' in rest) = 0
                         then length(rest)
                         else position(',' in rest) - 1 end),
         case when position(',' in rest) = 0 then ''
              else substring(rest from position(',' in rest) + 1) end
    from parts
   where rest <> ''
)
select value
  from parts
 where value <> '';

Book insight: string recipes often look like small utilities, but they are the building blocks for parsing serialized data, building reports, and cleaning imported files.

Takeaway: decide whether the string is a sequence, a delimited list, or a mixed-format record. The structure determines whether you need position arithmetic, recursive splitting, or a pattern match.

Chapter 7 · pages 191–226

Working with Numbers

Aggregation plus statistics: averages and counts, running totals/products, smoothing, mode and median, percentages, nullable columns, and anomaly detection.

What this chapter solves

Chapter 7 goes beyond basic aggregates. It covers running values, robust statistics, percentages, nullable columns, and anomaly checks such as median absolute deviation and Benford’s Law.

  • Average, minimum, maximum, sum, and counts.
  • Running totals and running products.
  • Mode, median, trimmed averages, and percentage of a total.
  • Outlier and anomaly detection with SQL-friendly formulas.

Core techniques

  • Window functions turn a running value into SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY ...).
  • Percentile functions or ordered subqueries implement median.
  • Join an aggregate back to detail rows when a percentage needs the grand total.
  • Exclude or down-weight extreme values when a robust estimate is required.

Dialect differences to expect

  • PERCENTILE_CONT/PERCENTILE_DISC support varies.
  • Integer division, NULL behavior, and rounding rules differ.
  • Window-frame syntax may be required for moving calculations.
  • Some engines provide MEDIAN or statistical helpers directly.

Common traps

  • Dividing by COUNT(*) when only non-NULL values should count.
  • Computing a running total without a deterministic ORDER BY.
  • Calling a mean “robust” even though one outlier can dominate it.
  • Confusing row count with distinct count in a joined aggregate.

Representative pattern

A running total is an ordered window aggregate. Partition when the sequence restarts, and always provide a unique ordering key.

select empno, hiredate, sal,
       sum(sal) over (order by hiredate, empno
                      rows between unbounded preceding
                              and current row) as running_sal
  from emp;

Book insight: the chapter mixes classic aggregation with statistical ideas. That combination is useful for data-quality checks as well as business reporting.

Takeaway: choose the statistic deliberately. A count, a mean, a median, and a robust estimate answer different questions—and the difference matters when NULLs or outliers are present.

Chapter 8 · pages 227–260

Date Arithmetic

Date intervals made explicit: adding and subtracting date parts, differences in multiple units, business-day counts, weekday occurrences, and gaps between neighboring records.

What this chapter solves

Chapter 8 is about intervals: add or subtract date parts, measure the distance between dates, count business days, and compare the current row with the next row in a series.

  • Add/subtract days, months, and years.
  • Calculate differences in days, months, years, hours, minutes, or seconds.
  • Count weekdays and business days in a period.
  • Find the gap between neighboring records.

Core techniques

  • Use date literals or DATE constructors to avoid ambiguous string formats.
  • Use DATEDIFF, -, INTERVAL, or vendor date functions as appropriate.
  • Generate a calendar/helper rowset when business-day counts need explicit weekend and holiday logic.
  • Use LAG/LEAD to compare a row with its neighbor.

Dialect differences to expect

  • Date-part names and rounding rules differ (MONTHS_BETWEEN, DATEADD, INTERVAL).
  • Some engines return a timestamp when you expect a date.
  • Business-day formulas must define whether the start/end dates are inclusive.
  • Time-zone and daylight-saving behavior can shift hour/second differences.

Common traps

  • Treating months as fixed 30-day blocks when the calendar says otherwise.
  • Counting a partial day as a full day in service-level calculations.
  • Using a locale-dependent string date such as '03/04/2026'.
  • Forgetting that date subtraction can include time-of-day fractions.

Representative pattern

When you need the time since the previous event, window functions keep the comparison in one query and avoid a self-join.

select event_id, event_time,
       event_time - lag(event_time)
                    over (order by event_time, event_id) as gap
  from events;

Book insight: date arithmetic is deceptively simple until calendars, business days, and partial timestamps enter the picture. The chapter’s examples make those edge cases explicit.

Takeaway: define the unit, the endpoints, and the rounding rule before writing the expression. For business-day questions, decide whether holidays and boundary days count.

Chapter 9 · pages 261–334

Date Manipulation

Calendars and date parts: leap-year logic, month and quarter boundaries, weekday occurrences, generated calendars, missing dates, date-part search, and overlapping ranges.

What this chapter solves

Chapter 9 manipulates dates rather than merely measuring them: leap years, month boundaries, weekday calendars, quarters, missing dates, date-part search, and overlapping ranges.

  • Determine leap years and days in a year.
  • Extract date units and find month/quarter boundaries.
  • Generate calendars and all occurrences of a weekday.
  • Fill gaps and compare ranges for overlap.

Core techniques

  • Construct dates from year/month/day components instead of parsing display strings.
  • Use DATE_TRUNC, DATEADD, LAST_DAY, or equivalent boundary functions.
  • Generate a date spine with a recursive CTE, GENERATE_SERIES, or a numbers table.
  • Test overlap with start1 < end2 and start2 < end1 (adjust inclusivity deliberately).

Dialect differences to expect

  • Week numbering and first-day-of-week settings vary by locale/engine.
  • Quarter functions are not available everywhere.
  • Interval arithmetic differs between +, DATEADD, and INTERVAL.
  • Some engines expose SERIES generators; others require recursion.

Common traps

  • Hard-coding 365/366 instead of testing the year.
  • Including an endpoint twice when a range is closed on both sides.
  • Filling dates only for existing groups and leaving absent groups empty.
  • Comparing a date column to a timestamp with an unexpected time component.

Representative pattern

A calendar is often a generated table of dates joined back to the fact table. That makes missing days visible instead of silently absent.

select c.day
  from calendar c
  left join sales s
    on s.sale_date = c.day
 where c.day between date '2026-01-01' and date '2026-01-31'
 order by c.day;

Book insight: date manipulation recipes are especially valuable for reporting calendars. Once dates are generated as rows, missing periods become a normal join problem.

Takeaway: normalize dates first, generate the calendar you need second, and join facts to that calendar third. Range overlap and missing-date questions then become straightforward comparisons.

Chapter 10 · pages 335–356

Working with Ranges

Gaps, islands, and continuity: consecutive runs, within-group differences, range boundaries, missing-value fills, and generated numeric sequences.

What this chapter solves

Chapter 10 is the gaps-and-islands toolbox: find consecutive runs, measure differences inside a group, mark range boundaries, fill missing values, and generate a clean numeric sequence.

  • Locate a range of consecutive values.
  • Compare each row with the previous row in its partition.
  • Find the first and last row of every run.
  • Fill holes and generate missing sequence numbers.

Core techniques

  • Row-number island method: row_number() - value is constant inside a consecutive run.
  • LAG/LEAD expose differences and boundary changes.
  • Partition by the business group before applying the sequence logic.
  • A generated numbers/date spine supplies missing members of a range.

Dialect differences to expect

  • Window functions are required for the cleanest solutions.
  • Sequence generators and recursive CTEs differ across engines.
  • Sorting rules can change what “consecutive” means for strings or dates.
  • Some databases provide native gap/level helpers, but the portable pattern is SQL.

Common traps

  • Forgetting PARTITION BY, so runs from different groups merge.
  • Assuming rows are returned in the order you expect without ORDER BY.
  • Filling numeric ranges but not date ranges (or vice versa).
  • Using duplicate ordering keys, which makes island boundaries unstable.

Representative pattern

For consecutive integers, subtract the row number from the value. The resulting constant identifies each island, making boundaries and lengths easy to aggregate.

select grp, min(val) as island_start,
       max(val) as island_end,
       count(*)  as island_size
  from (select grp, val,
               val - row_number() over (partition by grp
                                        order by val) as island_id
          from numbers) x
 group by grp, island_id
 order by grp, island_start;

Book insight: range problems look different in dates, identifiers, and inventory levels, but the underlying pattern is the same: impose an order, partition correctly, and detect where continuity breaks.

Takeaway: turn “consecutive” into an arithmetic relationship. Once a stable row number exists, gaps, islands, fills, and sequence generation all become variations of the same query.

Chapter 11 · pages 357–390

Advanced Searching

Pagination, top-n queries, rankings, shifted and reciprocal rows, duplicate suppression, knight-value lookups, and simple forecasts.

What this chapter solves

Chapter 11 tackles row-to-row and “top-n” questions: pagination, skipping rows, outer joins with OR logic, reciprocal matches, rankings, shifted values, forecasts, and the playful “knight value” problem.

  • Paginate or skip rows reliably.
  • Find top/bottom records and rank results.
  • Compare a row with future, previous, or reciprocal rows.
  • Suppress duplicates and produce simple forecasts.

Core techniques

  • ROW_NUMBER() creates stable pagination and de-duplication keys.
  • RANK/DENSE_RANK express business-friendly ordering.
  • LAG/LEAD shift values across rows.
  • Window functions avoid many self-joins, but a second pass is sometimes clearer.

Dialect differences to expect

  • Pagination syntax ranges from TOP to LIMIT to OFFSET ... FETCH.
  • Outer-join plus OR often needs an inline view or rewritten predicates.
  • Forecasting recipes are intentionally simple; production forecasting usually belongs outside SQL.
  • Ranking ties behave differently under RANK and DENSE_RANK.

Common traps

  • Paginating without a deterministic sort key.
  • Using WHERE RANK() = 1 in a query that also needs non-matching rows.
  • Assuming a “reciprocal” match is symmetric when the join columns are not.
  • Suppressing duplicates with DISTINCT when only one column should be unique.

Representative pattern

Rank first, then filter. This two-step shape handles “top n per group,” ties, and de-duplication without making the outer query repeat the window logic.

select *
  from (select deptno, ename, sal,
               row_number() over (partition by deptno
                                  order by sal desc, empno) as rn
          from emp) x
 where rn <= 3;

Book insight: the knight-value example is a memorable way to describe a two-step window lookup: first identify a target row, then read a different column from it.

Takeaway: most advanced search questions reduce to an ordering problem. Create a stable row number or rank, then filter or join on that derived value.

Chapter 12 · pages 391–456

Reporting and Reshaping

The report-building chapter: pivots and reverse pivots, repeated-value suppression, buckets, histograms, non-grouped columns, subtotals, sparse matrices, time grouping, and moving aggregates.

What this chapter solves

Chapter 12 turns query results into reports: pivot and unpivot, suppress repeated labels, bucket data, build histograms, calculate subtotals, flag rows, and aggregate over time windows.

  • Transpose rows into columns and back again.
  • Create fixed or predefined buckets and horizontal/vertical histograms.
  • Produce simple and multi-level subtotals.
  • Group by time units and compute moving-range aggregates.

Core techniques

  • Conditional aggregation: SUM(CASE ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) is the portable pivot.
  • GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, or CUBE create subtotal rows where supported.
  • Window functions handle moving sums and simultaneous partition aggregates.
  • Derived flags make sparse matrices and “is this a subtotal?” checks explicit.

Dialect differences to expect

  • Native PIVOT/UNPIVOT operators are vendor-specific.
  • Grouping-set syntax and grouping indicators differ across engines.
  • Percentages and rounding should be applied after the aggregate, not inside each bucket.
  • Time-bucket functions (DATE_TRUNC, FLOOR to interval) vary.

Common traps

  • Pivoting before filtering, so irrelevant categories create extra columns.
  • Losing the distinction between detail rows and subtotal rows.
  • Returning non-grouped columns without an agreed deterministic value.
  • Computing a histogram from a joined table and double-counting rows.

Representative pattern

Conditional aggregation keeps a pivot portable. One aggregate expression per output column turns the rows you care about into a single report row.

select deptno,
       sum(case when job = 'CLERK'   then 1 else 0 end) as clerks,
       sum(case when job = 'MANAGER' then 1 else 0 end) as managers,
       sum(case when job = 'ANALYST' then 1 else 0 end) as analysts
  from emp
 group by deptno
 order by deptno;

Book insight: the authors frame reshaping as the bridge between stored data and what users actually need to read—and as a foundation for data-warehouse-style presentations.

Takeaway: decide the report’s row grain first. Then pivot, subtotal, or bucket that grain explicitly; do not let joins or grouping silently change what one row means.

Chapter 13 · pages 457–480

Hierarchical Queries

Parent/child relationships in SQL: self-joins, recursive CTEs, indented hierarchy views, descendant searches, and root/branch/leaf classification.

What this chapter solves

Chapter 13 handles parent/child data: show managers and reports, walk several levels, render an entire hierarchy, collect all descendants, and classify nodes as root, branch, or leaf.

  • Join a child row to its immediate parent.
  • Traverse child → parent → grandparent chains.
  • Produce an indented or path-style hierarchy.
  • Find every descendant of a selected node.

Core techniques

  • A simple self-join covers one level.
  • A recursive CTE with an anchor and a recursive member covers unknown depth.
  • Carry depth and a path string to visualize or filter levels.
  • Node type is derived from parent/child existence, not stored as a label.

Dialect differences to expect

  • Recursive CTE syntax is standardized but cycle-handling options are not.
  • Oracle’s legacy CONNECT BY remains an alternative.
  • Path separators and indentation differ between reporting tools.
  • Some engines require explicit data types in the anchor member.

Common traps

  • Writing a recursive query without a termination condition for cycles.
  • Assuming every node has a parent (roots break naive joins).
  • Mixing depth and path logic, which makes levels hard to filter.
  • Using DISTINCT to hide duplicate paths caused by bad relationships.

Representative pattern

The anchor finds the starting node; the recursive member repeatedly joins the accumulated result back to the base table. Depth increments until no new rows appear.

with hierarchy (empno, ename, mgr, depth) as (
  select empno, ename, mgr, 0
    from emp
   where mgr is null
  union all
  select e.empno, e.ename, e.mgr, h.depth + 1
    from emp e
    join hierarchy h on e.mgr = h.empno
)
select * from hierarchy order by depth, ename;

Book insight: the chapter’s summary notes that standardized CTEs made hierarchical queries far more achievable across database vendors.

Takeaway: use a self-join for one level and a recursive CTE for the whole tree. Always carry depth or path information if users need to understand or filter the hierarchy.

Chapter 14 · pages 481–528

Odds ’n’ Ends

Vendor-specific and advanced leftovers: SQL Server pivot/unpivot, Oracle MODEL, unfixed string parsing, binary conversion, ranked/double pivots, serialized rows, percentages, and group-existence flags.

What this chapter solves

Chapter 14 gathers the vendor-specific and miscellaneous recipes: native pivot operators, Oracle’s MODEL clause, string parsing from unfixed locations, binary conversion, ranked pivots, serialized data, percentages, and group-existence flags.

  • Pivot/unpivot with SQL Server or reshape with Oracle MODEL.
  • Parse logs and serialized strings into usable rows or columns.
  • Build ranked pivots and double-pivoted reports with headers.
  • Calculate percentages and test whether a value exists within a group.

Core techniques

  • Native operators are convenient when available, but portable CASE aggregation remains a fallback.
  • Delimiter positions, recursive CTEs, and pattern matching turn serialized text into rows.
  • Rank first, then pivot or filter the ranked result.
  • Join a group-level flag back to detail rows to test existence without changing grain.

Dialect differences to expect

  • SQL Server PIVOT/UNPIVOT and Oracle MODEL are not portable.
  • Oracle functions such as binary conversion and composite-subquery tricks are vendor-specific.
  • String parsing functions differ in indexing, escaping, and regex support.
  • Percent calculations need an explicit denominator and rounding policy.

Common traps

  • Assuming a native pivot will preserve the same row order as a CASE version.
  • Parsing serialized data without handling empty or missing fields.
  • Ranking ties inconsistently before a pivot.
  • Testing group existence with an aggregate that changes the detail row grain.

Representative pattern

When a vendor gives you a pivot operator, use it for readability—but keep the portable conditional-aggregation form in mind for migrations and cross-platform code.

-- portable fallback for a SQL Server-style pivot
select deptno,
       max(case when job = 'CLERK'   then sal end) as clerk_sal,
       max(case when job = 'MANAGER' then sal end) as manager_sal
  from emp
 group by deptno;

Book insight: this chapter is the toolbox for the last mile of a query: the moment a standard pattern meets a specific engine’s syntax or a messy real-world data format.

Takeaway: isolate vendor-specific features behind a small query boundary. The surrounding logic—ranking, grouping, percentages, and row grain—should remain portable.

Appendix A · pages 529–556

Window Function Refresher

A compact review of grouping versus windowing, partitions, ordering, frames, and the aggregate/ranking/offset functions used throughout the book.

What this appendix refreshes

Appendix A is a compact refresher on window functions—the engine behind many later recipes. It separates ordinary grouping from windowed calculations and reviews the main function families.

  • GROUP BY collapses rows; window functions keep row detail.
  • PARTITION BY defines independent calculation groups.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER defines sequence and frame.
  • Aggregate, ranking, and offset functions share the same window frame.

Function families

  • Aggregate windows: SUM, COUNT, AVG, MIN, MAX.
  • Ranking windows: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK.
  • Offset windows: LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE.
  • Frames: ROWS or RANGE bounds around the current row.

Key mental model

  • Filtering with WHERE happens before window evaluation.
  • Window results are computed after the base result set is formed.
  • An empty OVER() means “the whole result set.”
  • A missing ORDER BY makes row order and frames nondeterministic.

Common traps

  • Filtering on a window function in the same WHERE clause.
  • Using an aggregate without a frame when a moving range was intended.
  • Confusing RANK gaps with DENSE_RANK continuity.
  • Assuming partition order is stable without a unique tie-breaker.

Representative pattern

Partition for independent groups, order for sequence, and use a frame when the calculation should include only neighboring rows.

select deptno, ename, sal,
       sum(sal) over (partition by deptno) as dept_total,
       sum(sal) over (partition by deptno
                      order by hiredate, empno
                      rows between unbounded preceding
                              and current row) as running_dept_total
  from emp;

  • Windowing · p.541

Book insight: the appendix is the bridge from classic aggregation to the modern window-function recipes used throughout Chapters 7, 10, 11, and 12.

Takeaway: before writing a window expression, answer three questions: what is the partition, what is the order, and what is the frame?
Appendix B · pages 557–560

Common Table Expressions

A short guide to named intermediate results: subqueries versus CTEs, composition, readability, and the recursive pattern used for hierarchies and generated sequences.

What this appendix adds

Appendix B introduces common table expressions (CTEs) as a readability layer over subqueries. It compares the two forms and points toward recursive CTEs for hierarchy and sequence problems.

  • Named, reusable result sets make long queries easier to follow.
  • Multiple CTEs can be composed in a logical order.
  • Recursive CTEs provide a standardized way to walk trees and generate series.

Subquery vs. CTE

  • Subquery: compact and local, but repeated expressions can become nested and hard to read.
  • CTE: named and staged, which helps debugging and reuse within one statement.
  • Materialization: engines may or may not optimize CTEs like views or inline tables.
  • Recursion: a CTE is the portable home for anchor + recursive-member logic.

Practical guidance

  • Use a CTE when a derived result is referenced more than once or needs a clear name.
  • Keep each CTE to one conceptual step: filter, rank, aggregate, then present.
  • For recursion, include a termination condition and guard against cycles.
  • Prefer portable constructs when the query must run on several databases.

Representative pattern

A CTE names the intermediate result before the final projection. The same query can often be rewritten as nested subqueries, but the named form reads more like a small program.

with top_salaries as (
  select deptno, ename, sal,
         row_number() over (partition by deptno
                            order by sal desc, empno) as rn
    from emp
)
select deptno, ename, sal
  from top_salaries
 where rn <= 3;

Book insight: CTEs are the readability companion to window functions: both let you express multi-step analysis without hiding the steps inside deeply nested expressions.

Takeaway: name the intermediate result. A CTE is not a new kind of calculation—it is a clearer way to stage the calculations you already know.
